Waiting prepares witnesses for a task larger than their question

The apostles ask about timing in verse 6. Will the kingdom come back to Israel now? Verse 7 says the times are not theirs to know. Verse 8 gives them a task in place of a date. Power will come with the Holy Spirit, not from their own plan. The task moves outward: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, then the ends of the earth. Verse 22 defines a witness: one who saw Jesus from John’s baptism onward.
Many languages lead toward shared life

The hearers are cut to the heart and ask what to do (verse 37). Verse 38 answers with repentance, baptism, and the gift of the Holy Spirit. Verse 39 says how far that gift reaches. It is for the hearers, their children, and all who are far off. Joel’s words in verse 17 already said “all flesh.” The list of nations in verses 9–11 shows who is listening. The limit in verse 39 is God’s call, not place or birth.
A healing redirects attention away from the healers

The crowd runs to Peter and John in wonder (verse 11). Verse 12 asks why, and it names their wrong guess. They think the two men’s own power or godliness made him walk. Verse 13 gives the credit to the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Verse 16 says faith in Jesus’ name made the man strong. Peter speaks to this crowd about its own acts (verses 13–15). Verse 17 then says they acted in ignorance, and verse 19 offers repentance.
A visible witness limits the council's threat

The council has a problem in verses 14–16. The healed man stands there, and all Jerusalem knows the sign. They cannot deny it, so they try to stop the speech (verse 17). Verse 19 asks them to judge: listen to them or to God. Verse 20 gives the reason the order cannot work. The two men saw and heard these things themselves. Verse 21 shows the result: the council threatens and lets them go.
Deceit threatens trust within a sharing community

Chapter 4 ended with Barnabas giving the full price of a field. Ananias brings a part and lets it stand as the whole (verses 1–2). Verse 4 makes clear what the wrong is. The land was his, and the money was his to use. No rule made him give it all. The wrong is the lie, and verse 4 says it was told to God. Verse 11 reports the result: great fear on the whole assembly.
Unequal care produces a shared decision

The complaint in verse 1 is about daily help for widows. The twelve say they should not leave the word to serve tables (verse 2). Verse 3 gives the choice to the whole group. It also sets the test: good report, the Spirit, and wisdom. The apostles keep prayer and the word as their own work (verse 4). Verse 5 says the plan pleased the whole group, and it names the seven. Verse 7 reports the result: the word of God increased.
Stephen's answer follows rejected helpers and God's wider presence

Stephen is charged with speaking against the holy place (6:13–14). His answer shows God at work far from it. God acts in Mesopotamia (verse 2), Egypt (verse 9), and Sinai (verse 30). Verse 33 calls desert ground holy. Verse 48 then says the Most High does not live in houses made by hands. Verses 49–50 quote Isaiah: heaven is God’s throne, and his hand made all things. The charge is about a place, and the answer is about where God is.
Scattering brings witness and a question about Scripture

The official has the scroll and reads it aloud (verses 28 and 30). Philip asks if he understands. Verse 31 says he cannot without a guide, and he invites Philip up. His question in verse 34 is exact: does the prophet mean himself or another? Philip starts from that passage and tells him about Jesus (verse 35). Simon wanted to buy a power (verses 18–19). The official asks for an explanation, and then for baptism (verse 36).
Saul's changed direction requires other people's trust

The Lord tells Ananias to go to Saul (verse 11). Verse 13 is his objection: many have reported Saul’s evil in Jerusalem. Verse 14 adds that Saul holds authority to bind believers in Damascus too. The Lord does not deny the reports. He calls Saul a chosen vessel (verse 15). Ananias goes and calls him “Brother Saul” (verse 17). In verses 26–27 the disciples fear Saul until Barnabas speaks for him.
The Spirit's arrival changes Peter's judgment

Peter says in verse 28 that a Jew may not visit another nation. God has shown him to call no person unclean. Verse 34 states the lesson: God does not show favoritism. Verses 44–46 then give proof that the Jewish believers can hear. The Gentiles speak in other languages and praise God. Verse 47 asks a question that expects no objection. They have the Spirit “just like us,” so water cannot be refused.
Peter must explain the meal and the shared gift

The charge in verse 3 is about a meal, not about baptism. Peter answers in order (verse 4), and he lists what God did. The vision came three times (verse 10). The Spirit told him to go (verse 12). The Spirit fell as he began to speak (verse 15). Verse 17 ends with a question: who was he to stand against God? Verse 18 shows the hearers accept it: God gave repentance to the Gentiles too.
An opened prison meets a closed household gate

Verse 5 says the assembly prayed constantly for Peter. Verse 12 shows many still praying when he knocks. Yet verse 15 has them call Rhoda crazy. Then they say it must be his angel. They prayed for him and did not expect him at the gate. Peter himself thought the rescue was a vision (verse 9). Verse 16 ends it plainly: they open the gate, see him, and are amazed.
A synagogue invitation becomes a dispute over wider hearing

The first Sabbath ends well: many Jews and converts follow Paul (verse 43). The turn comes in verses 44–45, when the whole city gathers. Verse 45 says jealousy at the crowds moved those who contradicted him. Verse 46 answers that group in that city. The word had to come to them first, and they pushed it away. Verse 47 quotes Isaiah on a light for the Gentiles. Paul still starts in the synagogue in the next city (14:1).
Praise and violence both misunderstand the visiting teachers

The crowd explains the healing in its own terms: gods have come down (verse 11). Verse 15 refuses the honor in two steps. The two are men “of the same nature” as the crowd. Their news is to turn from these things to the living God. Paul quotes no Scripture in this speech. He points to the maker of sky, earth, and sea. Verse 17 names the witness this crowd already has: rain, harvests, and food.
A disputed requirement leads to a letter and trusted messengers

The question in verses 1 and 5 is whether Gentiles must keep Moses’ law. Peter calls that a yoke their fathers could not bear (verse 10). Verse 28 gives the answer in the letter’s own words. It names two who agree: the Holy Spirit and “us.” The word “burden” answers Peter’s “yoke.” Only four things remain, listed in verse 29. Verse 31 shows how the readers took it: they rejoiced at the encouragement.
Lost income becomes a public charge and a prison crisis

The jailer was ordered to keep them safely (verse 23). Verse 27 shows what open doors mean to him. He thinks the prisoners are gone, and he draws his sword on himself. Verse 28 stops him with a fact: all are still there. The men he chained now save his life. His question in verse 30 follows: what must he do to be saved? Verses 33–34 show the change: he washes their wounds and feeds them.
Paul changes his starting point for different hearers

In the synagogue Paul argues from the Scriptures (verses 2–3). At the Areopagus he quotes no Scripture. Verse 23 starts with an altar of the Athenians’ own. Its words admit there is a god they do not know. Paul says he will announce that one. He then quotes their poets, not the prophets (verse 28). Verse 31 ends with the same claim: God raised a man from the dead.
Teaching develops through work, hospitality, and correction

Verses 24–25 praise Apollos first. He is eloquent, strong in the Scriptures, and accurate about Jesus. One thing is missing: he knows only the baptism of John. Verse 26 shows how the gap is closed. Priscilla and Aquila hear him and take him aside. They explain the way of God “more accurately.” Verses 27–28 show the result: he greatly helps the believers in Achaia.
Changed worship threatens a trade and gathers a confused crowd

Verse 25 opens Demetrius’s speech with money. The craftsmen have their wealth from this business. Verse 26 names the threat: Paul says gods made by hands are no gods. Only in verse 27 does he add the honor of Artemis and her temple. The crowd takes up the second reason and shouts her name (verse 28). Verse 32 says most did not know why they had come. The clerk points them to the courts (verses 35–38).
Paul's farewell makes care more important than personal gain

Paul warns in verses 29–30 that some will draw disciples after themselves. Verse 33 sets his own record against that. He wanted no one’s silver, gold, or clothing. Verse 34 says his own hands paid for him and his companions. Verse 35 turns that record into a pattern for the elders. They are to work so that they can help the weak. The saying of Jesus gives the reason: giving is more blessed than receiving.
Warnings and an untested accusation lead toward arrest

Verse 28 makes two charges: Paul teaches against the temple and brought Greeks in. Verse 29 gives the basis for the second charge. The accusers saw Trophimus with Paul in the city. They “supposed” the rest. Paul was in fact there to complete a purification (verse 26). Verse 34 shows the crowd’s state: the officer could not learn the facts.
Paul's defense reaches its breaking point with the Gentile task

The crowd listens through the whole account of Jesus’ voice and Ananias. Verse 22 says they listened “until he said that.” The breaking point is verse 21, not the vision. Paul says the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles. He says this came while he prayed in the temple (verse 17). He even objected that Jerusalem knew his past (verses 19–20). The crowd in 21:28 already charged him with bringing Greeks in.
A promise of Rome passes through a divided hearing and a hidden plot

Verse 10 leaves Paul in the barracks after a hearing that settled nothing. The officer feared he would be torn apart. Verse 11 comes that night and gives the one fixed point. As he testified in Jerusalem, he must testify in Rome. A sworn plot tests that word at once (verses 12–13). The way out is ordinary: a nephew hears and reports (verse 16). Verse 23 sends Paul out alive under 470 guards.
A delayed hearing preserves the governor's advantage

Felix knows the Way well and still delays the ruling (verse 22). Verse 25 shows one reason. Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control, and judgment, and Felix is terrified. Verse 26 gives a second reason, and it is money. He hopes Paul will pay for release, so he sends for him often. Verse 27 adds a third: he wants favor with Paul’s accusers. After two years Paul is still bound, with no ruling given.
Paul's appeal creates a journey without a clear written charge

Paul’s appeal in verse 11 binds Festus to send him (verse 12). That leaves the governor with a letter he cannot write. Verse 25 says he found nothing deserving death. Verse 26 says he has nothing certain to write to the emperor. Verse 19 shows why: the dispute is about Jesus, whom Paul says is alive. Verse 27 states the difficulty in Festus’s own words. A prisoner sent with no charge makes no sense, so he asks Agrippa’s help.
Paul answers a royal hearing by inviting belief

Paul is the one on trial, yet verse 27 questions the king. Agrippa answers that Paul is trying to make him a Christian (verse 28). Verse 29 takes that answer and widens it. Paul wishes it for Agrippa and for all who hear him. He wants them to be as he is, with one thing left out. “Except for these bonds” points to the chains he wears. Verse 31 gives the hearers’ verdict: nothing he did deserves death or bonds.
Promised survival still requires food, sailors, and restraint

Verse 24 promises that all who sail with Paul will live. Verse 30 then shows sailors lowering the boat to escape. Verse 31 says the soldiers cannot be saved unless the sailors stay. The promise does not remove the need for the crew. The soldiers believe Paul this time and cut the ropes (verse 32). In verse 11 the centurion had trusted the pilot over him. Verse 44 reports the result: all escape safely to land.
The ending leaves Paul bound while teaching continues

The book has moved toward Rome since 23:11. It does not report the hearing before Caesar. Verse 30 says Paul stayed two years in a rented house. Verse 16 says a soldier guarded him. Verse 31 says what he did there: he taught about God’s kingdom and Jesus. The last words are “without hindrance.” Paul is held, but the teaching is not.
